wordsPreamble:
- English, with an Ulster accent that runs fast and moves its vowels around. Irish and Ulster Scots turn up on some signs; neither is widely spoken day to day.
- Belfast is friendly and direct, and strangers will talk to you at bus stops. The humour is dry and teasing, and being slagged off by a new friend is a good sign.
- Words carry sides here. Place names, flags, football shirts and Derry versus Londonderry all signal something, so follow how the person you’re talking to says it.
- Prices are in pounds sterling. Northern Irish banks print their own notes, which look unfamiliar but spend the same.

words.context: Universal across Northern Ireland, from bus drivers to bank managers.
Not at all is the standard reply to thanks, and means you’re welcome rather than no.
The usual thanks at a bar or counter. Thanks very much is the fuller form.
A greeting, not a question, usually squashed to ’bout ye. “Not bad, yourself?” closes it.
Still current here. Bye is often said several times in a row on the way out the door.
The same reflex as Britain. Also means “pardon?”
Bar service runs on eye contact and patience. The bar staff know who came in when.

words.groupNote: Sorry covers both apology and getting past. Excuse me opens a request.

words.context: Can I get passes here without comment. A wee one of anything is also understood.
Class works among younger people: that was class means excellent.
Asking for the check marks you instantly.
Less common than in London and usually only for big groups. Check the bill before you tip around 10%.
Translink Metro buses and the Glider take contactless. On the Glider you pay at the stop, not on board.
Loo works. The bogs is cruder and common. Restroom gets a blank look.
Northern Irish banks print their own sterling notes. They’re valid across the UK but shops in England sometimes refuse them.
Contactless everywhere. Say it as you hold the card up.
Still useful at St George’s Market stalls and in older pubs.
Charged since 2013. Say no thanks if you brought one.
Small, and also a softener attached to almost anything. A wee cup of tea, a wee minute, a wee drive to Bangor, which is not that wee.
Fine, sound, agreed. He’s dead on is a compliment; dead on, see you at eight settles a plan. Dead on its own just means very.
Get a grip, don’t be ridiculous. Said to someone talking nonsense, usually with a laugh, sometimes without one.
Mortified, deeply embarrassed. The feeling of waving back at someone who was waving at the person behind you.
Northern Ireland, said fast in a Belfast accent and written down as a joke. Mostly heard from football fans and on the terraces at Windsor Park stadium.
